author: Mo Qureshi
headline: Automotive features on the Saudi Industry Forum agenda in Jeddah
deck: Saudi Arabia has committed to vehicle manufacturing at scale, and the supplier base it requires does not yet exist.
excerpt: Automotive forms one of the Saudi Industry Forum's nine programme axes, against a vehicle manufacturing programme still working toward its first substantial output.
content:
Automotive is among the nine declared programme axes at the Saudi Industry Forum in Jeddah from 14 September. It is the axis with the widest gap between national commitment and current output.

Saudi Arabia has targeted more than 300,000 vehicles a year by 2030, resting on three plants that have to deliver it, and this publication has reported that the Kingdom's car plants have reached the year in which they have to start working. Lucid has pushed full Saudi production into 2027 as it reset spending. Ceer has signed localisation deals worth SAR 9.2bn as it builds a supplier base.

The supplier base is the substance of the challenge and the reason automotive belongs on an industrial forum agenda rather than only in an investment one. A vehicle assembly plant is the visible end of a supply chain containing thousands of components, most of which are made by tier one and tier two suppliers located close to the assembly line because the logistics of shipping them long distances erodes the economics. Building an assembly plant without that supplier ecosystem produces an operation importing kits, which delivers employment and very little industrial depth.

Establishing the ecosystem is a chicken-and-egg problem that every emerging automotive nation has faced. Component suppliers invest where there is assembly volume; assemblers locate where there are suppliers. Breaking the deadlock requires either the assembler committing volume ahead of the suppliers existing — which is what Ceer's localisation agreements attempt — or the state underwriting the gap.

The Kingdom's advantages are real: petrochemical feedstock for plastics and composites, growing steel and aluminium capacity, low energy costs, and a domestic market of meaningful size. The disadvantages are equally real: no existing automotive engineering workforce at scale, no established tier two base, and competition from mature supplier networks in Turkey, Eastern Europe and Asia that can serve the same market at lower cost.

The Jeddah location gives the axis a particular relevance. The western region's manufacturing base is oriented toward consumer goods rather than heavy engineering, and the automotive programme is concentrated elsewhere. What a Jeddah forum can usefully address is whether western-region manufacturers can qualify into the supplier base — which is a question about certification, quality systems and volume commitment rather than about capability in principle.

This publication has reported the wider pattern in Saudi localisation: the categories that move are those with volume, stable specification and repeat orders. Automotive components fit that description well, which is what makes the programme plausible if the volume arrives.

Programme axes are taken from the organiser's published material.
